Apologies if you're replying to the article, but If this is addressed to me: to categorize my dislike of MS's offerings as some kind of hypocrisy is a judgement made ill-informed of my own principles.

First, I don't use nor endorse a single Apple product and never will. I think their control of their ecosystem is consumer unfriendly. Google's Android is okay on my phone for at least the reason that if I did want to do something beyond making a call or navigating, I can use alternative app markets or install APKs. This is a check&balance that allows consumers to circumvent Google if they were to abuse the power granted by the wide adoption of their app store.

The problem with Microsoft's "walled garden" is that MS is introducing the concept of an app market for Windows while simultaneously positioning themselves as the only market on the platform. I'd prefer that they release an API that allows the creation of independent app markets and for consumers to easily connect with.

Why? Because the best case scenario for MS here is that all Windows users become dependent on their new app store, but practically speaking let's say it's only a large percentage of users like 80%. At that saturation point, a lot of new software would become app-market-install-only because the developers would have to choose to spend their resources on an installer (for 20% of the user base, and find their own way to market their software) or the app market (for 80% of the user base becoming aware just by going to the app market). And let's say MS did some really bad censoring with their market at the height of its saturation, it'd take a lot of resources on the parts of developers and momentum on the parts of consumers to actually move away from it at that point. What does all that result in? MS having a lot of power on what software their consumers are likely to ever use.

For a recent example of what it looks like when companies abuse this, see Apple kicking out even educational games regarding the civil war because they displayed a confederate flag. They only added them back after they got all sorts of bad publicity about it in the news. But what if it were a smaller app, that fewer people were to know about? What if it were your app they removed because they thought your content or functionality was unwanted? It's a slippery slope once you say it's okay to censor content for you, and that is the power Apple has and MS would effectively have it too in the scenario I describe.

For the past few years I've been moving more and more towards Linux precisely because I've grown to find MS as distasteful as Apple and Google in some very key ways (and possibly increasing as it seems like they just play copycat so much now). I don't value an exchange of convenience at the sake of consumer protection, especially when we could be given both.

Thomas A. Johnson packed up his car that misty September morning. It had been drizzling down the icy rain all week. Hoping the roads weren't too terrible, he kissed his fiance goodbye - he told her he was off to catch up with an old friend. It was a half truth, but still, he felt terrible lying to her.

But she never questioned him. He figured she knew the truth, but he wasn't going to mention it if she wouldn't.

Turning on his headlights and windshield wipers, Tom drove the 400 or so miles to his cabin by the lakeside. The cabin, larger than most in the area, was rarely used save for these special occasions. The storm, only getting worse, threw down heavy drops of rain onto the roof of his car. The thudding of the water lightened a little as he turned off his car and removed the keys from the ignition.

Tommy stepped out of the car and walked to the long, narrow dock. If it lightened up, maybe he could go fishing tomorrow, but it wasn't likely. The dark grey thunderhead loomed off in the west, moving quickly toward him. He stared at the usually placid lake and each drop of rain hitting the surface, and splashing back up. His clothes, now drenched and heavy with the near-autumn water, didn't seem to bother him. After a minute or so, he headed back to his car, unloaded his suitcase and walked up to the solid cabin door.

Entering, Tom threw the keys onto the little table by the door, clanking and scattering until they came to a rest. He plopped the suitcase down and opened it. He cast aside his drenched clothes and dried off with a towel. Wrapping it around his waist, Tom passed over to the fireplace, lit a match, and began to stoke a fire.

After the glowing embers burst into flame, he walked back over to his suitcase and retrieved his best suit. He wore it every time. Crossing over to the bathroom, he changed and slicked back his still wet hair into a neat part. He tied the thin black tie around his neck, and went to the kitchen cupboard.

He retrieved two glasses, two cigars from his humidifier, and an Old bottle of Four Roses. Carrying it all back to the fireplace, he poured the two drinks and sat one down next to the empty seat beside him. He sunk into the chair, holding his beverage. He was silent for awhile, the crackling fire and the pounding rain the only sounds on the late summer night.

"Four Roses - No ice. Just how you like it," Tommy paused, "It's been 16 years, Jim." Tom sighed, looking at the empty seat. He cut the two cigars, placing one near the place where his friend should have sat. He took a puff of the oakey tobacco. Silence fell again.

"...Gettin' married next month. But you know that. I have a fine gal. You didn't get to meet her -- thank god, you'd've just taken her right away from me," Tommy forced a laugh. "You always were the charmer. But let me tell you -- this gal is a fiery one. Eleanor's her name --- I call her Ellie though. Pretty too, long brown hair and those blue eyes like lightning. 'Bout time I got hitched, don't ya think, Jimmy?"

Another long pause of silence was broken by the clap of thunder, accompanied by whistling wind and banging shutters. He polished off his bourbon and poured another. He repeated this four times.

"And you know what? You shoulda been there. Be my best man. Get married, have kids, all that shit. But you're not here because you were fucking stupid and had to be a GODDAMNED HERO." Tommy didn't know why he was shouting at the air. His chest began to feel heavy with the familiar pangs of grief that'd stricken him for the past 16 years. On his face, Tommy could feel the white-hot tears stinging his eyes, wanting to escape. Finally, the tears poured out as his shaky hands tried to hold the liquor glass.

"You're not here. And it's so damn hard bein' happy, Jimmy. I feel.... I feel guilty. Every time I get to see Ellie, every time I get a raise, and I'm so damn guilty -" Tom's voice cracked at he stared at the seat. "You shoulda been the one here. Not me. Not me."

Tom closed his eyes, trying to quell the aching feeling in his head -- he could hear the blood thumping through his temple.

"You had to jump on it, didn't you, Jim?" Tommy pulled out a photo of Jimmy and him in their Army fatigues -- just hours before their trench was bombed. Sgt. James B. Fredricks saw a live grenade land between them. As tommy remained, steadfast and shooting, Sgt. Fredricks pushed him out of the way and covered the grenade with his body.

The medics said he died almost instantly.

That was no comfort for Tommy, who held his bloody friend, covered in muck and debris, while he only suffered a shrapnel wound to the leg.

Tom closed his eyes again, trying to remember more, but everything was a blur.

"Jimmy..." He said softly, sipping on the bourbon. "Just so ya know, when I have a son he'll be Named James Bartholomew. I Know you hated that name. But you know what? It's gonna happen. I swear to god, when we meet again, Heaven or Hell, I'll make sure you'll kick me."

Tommy's hand went to his neck. He closed his hand around the silver dogtag. He didn't know when he'd make his peace with this. It'd been 16 years. Maybe it was the liquor, maybe it was the fireplace, but Tommy drifted off into sleep.

He opened his eyes the next morning, the sun peaking its way through the curtains.

"Well, Jim," Tommy got up and started to change. "Time to go fishing."

As he exited the room, he left the small glass of bourbon -- Four Roses, neat -- by the table. Just like he'd do every year.
